sentences.text: The complete skeleton of Helodus simplex is known from multiple articulated specimens, revealing an endoskeleton composed entirely of cartilage rather than bone.
Its first dorsal fin featured a short, smooth spine supported by the synarcual, a specialized structure at the base of the skull, and this spine was made of osteodentin, a tooth-like tissue.
Unlike most relatives of its group, Helodus simplex lived in a shallow freshwater environment.
The genus was originally named based on isolated bead-like teeth found in the late Paleozoic era.

Naturalist Louis Agassiz named the genus Helodus in 1838 based on isolated bead-like teeth from the late Paleozoic. James William Davis later described a fossil skeleton of Helodus simplex in 1890, which is now housed at the Hunterian Museum and Art Gallery. The first described skeleton of Helodus simplex was found in an ironstone mine in Staffordshire, England.
Helodus is the sole member of the family Helodontidae and the order Helodontiformes. It belongs to the class Chondrichthyes and the subclass Holocephali, which includes living chimaeras.

Fossils of Helodus date from the Late Devonian to the Early Permian periods. The time range for Helodus is from the Tournaisian to the Changhsingian, approximately 358.86 to 251.902 million years ago.

Over 70 species have been attributed to Helodus based on similar teeth, but these likely belong to many different unrelated fish groups, making the genus a 'wastebasket taxon'. Researchers have tentatively suggested a relationship between Helodus and the order Eugeneodontiformes based on tooth similarities, but this requires further confirmation.
